source.title: Understanding language model scaling for protein fitness prediction
source.authors: Chao Hou; Di Liu; Aziz Zafar; Yu-Feng Shen

record.file_problem: The text is a complete bioRxiv preprint and is not visibly cut off or garbled. Its title differs from the supplied title, and the text gives a 2025 preprint DOI rather than the supplied identifier.
record.tranche_reason: Evaluates whether scaling in protein language models predicts downstream mutation-effect performance, extending the downstream-predictability question to protein models and a protein-specific task.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates ESM2 protein-model size, masked-residue perplexity, and mutation-effect prediction. It reports lower perplexity for larger models but does not fit or test power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute; it has no token or compute sweep or compute-optimal allocation test. Values in the figures are not transcribed numerically in the text. The downstream performance findings and the explicitly described qualitative comparisons are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The study measures zero-shot mutation-effect performance across ESM2 sizes (8M–15B) and against per-protein masked perplexity. These are its own results on whether downstream performance improves with scale or lower loss (V6), in a new setting: protein LMs. It fits no power laws and has no token or compute sweep, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find ESM2 mutation-effect performance peaks at per-protein perplexity 3–6, so the largest models are not always best. Very high or very low perplexity collapses the LLR dynamic range. They attribute the large-model decline to overfitting: memorising wild-type residues rather than conservation profiles. They argue mutation-effect prediction may be a poor benchmark for perplexity-minimising pLMs. They suggest switching to smaller models, or fine-tuning, according to perplexity, and propose excluding low-perplexity proteins during training.
record.recipe_differences: Uses masked-residue protein perplexity and zero-shot mutation-effect LLR evaluation across ESM2 sizes; does not fit language-model loss scaling laws or test compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Mutation-effect performance varies with protein-level perplexity; the reported peak is at 3–6, and performance declines below that range, especially in larger models and proteins with sufficient homologs.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger ESM2 models consistently reach lower median masked-residue perplexity on both datasets. No power law is fitted, and this is downstream-protein perplexity rather than held-out pretraining loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Masked-residue perplexity of protein LMs on benchmark proteins decreases monotonically with ESM2 size.

record.peer_reviewed: preprint; text states it was not certified by peer review
record.problems: The scaling-related values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The study tests only ESM2 protein models and protein mutation-effect tasks, and does not fit scaling laws or evaluate tokens and compute. The four-protein LLR examples are qualitative and do not identify the medium-sized checkpoints.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported results bearing on V6 were left out. Figures 1 and S1 also show curves and per-protein points without numerical values; the recorded rows preserve the explicitly described aggregate trends rather than extracting individual plotted points.

untested.parts: Text language models; downstream tasks other than zero-shot protein mutation-effect prediction; any quantitative predictive fit of downstream performance against scale or loss.
No power-law fit and no token or compute sweep. R1/R2 show only that perplexity falls monotonically with ESM2 size.
Protein LMs are used, but no power-law form is tested.

missing.what: The performance decline at low perplexity appears mainly in larger models and in proteins with many training homologs. Small models show no decline, and proteins with few homologs never reach low perplexity.
Viral and designed proteins perform consistently worse even at comparable perplexity. Perplexity does not predict downstream performance out of distribution.
Per-protein perplexity correlates with the number of homologs in UniRef50.

record.verdict_notes: The text is the bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2025.04.25.650688), not the supplied Nature Computational Science DOI. All values are figure-only, and states rest on the authors' qualitative statements. The Figure 2 proteins were chosen because they show the rise-then-fall pattern. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits; no sweep over training tokens or compute; the study does not establish whether held-out protein perplexity follows a power law in model size.
No fits on small runs or predictions for larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation study or parameter/token allocation fits.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study uses protein language models, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in protein or other modalities or training regimes.
Tests zero-shot protein mutation-effect prediction with ESM2 and protein perplexity; it does not test downstream tasks for text language models or a broad range of downstream tasks.

No fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across fitting choices. The study's non-monotonic downstream results concern mutation-effect prediction, not bending of a fitted pretraining-loss power law.
